query: For HfNbTaTiZr refractory high-entropy alloy, earlier studies separately examined tensile creep at 1250 °C, microhardness changes during cold rolling, elastic moduli from 293 to 1100 K, and hardening after aging at 600–800 °C. However, these findings do not provide a unified explanation of the alloy’s stress–strain and thermoelastic behavior. Thermal expansion is also relevant because mismatch can produce thermal stresses during composite solidification and potentially affect strength. What single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain the unresolved behavior? Specify a controlled comparison that would isolate the governing cause, observations predicted relative to a baseline, the relevant temperature and response boundaries, how the earlier findings support the hypothesis, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: A temperature-dependent, reversible short-range ordering (SRO) of chemically distinct, B2-like Hf/Zr-rich and Nb/Ta/Ti-rich clusters forms in equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr between ≈600 °C and ≈900 °C, increases the alloy’s resistance to dislocation glide (raising hardness and modulus), and generates internal mismatch stresses that modify the thermoelastic response; the SRO dissolves above ≈1100 °C, eliminating the obstacles and permitting rapid dislocation climb that dominates the 1250 °C creep rate.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr refractory high-entropy alloy, single-phase bcc, ~30 µm grains, solution-quenched from 1200 °C to minimise prior SRO.
generation.intervention: Isothermal aging at 700 °C for 24 h (to promote SRO) versus immediate water quench from 1200 °C (random solid solution baseline).
generation.conditions: Subsequent tests: (i) room-temperature microhardness, (ii) resonant ultrasound modulus measurements from 25 °C to 1000 °C on heating, (iii) constant-stress tensile creep at 1250 °C/150 MPa for 20 h, all in high-vacuum to minimise oxidation.
generation.structural_mediator: Number density and correlation length of B2-like SRO clusters (1–3 nm) quantified by diffuse synchrotron/X-ray/neutron scattering during and after aging.
generation.mechanism: 1. At 600–900 °C chemical SRO lowers stacking fault energy locally and produces Å-scale lattice distortions that raise Peierls barriers, increasing hardness and elastic moduli; 2. Thermal-expansion mismatch between SRO clusters and the surrounding random matrix adds internal stresses, giving an anomalous temperature dependence of modulus; 3. Above ~1100 °C the SRO dissolves, removing these obstacles so dislocation climb and glide dominate, leading to the measured high creep rates at 1250 °C; 4. Cold rolling supplies excess dislocations that catalyse SRO formation on subsequent moderate-temperature exposure, explaining extra work-hardening reported earlier.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the quenched baseline, 700 °C-aged specimens will show: • ≈20–30 % higher room-temperature Vickers hardness; • ≈10 % higher shear modulus up to ~800 °C, followed by a sharper drop (≥5 %) between 900 and 1100 °C as SRO dissolves; • An initially lower creep strain rate (≥3× reduction) during the first hour at 1250 °C, converging to the baseline rate after SRO fully disorders (verified by in-situ scattering).
generation.baseline: Water-quenched, SRO-free HfNbTaTiZr tested under identical thermal-mechanical histories.
generation.boundary: Hypothesis expected to hold for 0.2 ≤ c_i ≤ 0.25 of each element (near-equiatomic), grain sizes 5–100 µm, and temperatures 500–1100 °C where SRO is thermodynamically stable; outside this range (e.g., <500 °C or >1100 °C long exposures) no significant SRO effects are predicted.
generation.uncertainty: Magnitude of modulus jump and exact SRO stability window may vary with impurity (O, N) level; competing mechanisms such as ω-phase precipitation or interstitial segregation could also contribute and need to be excluded.

falsification_experiment.design: In-situ high-energy X-ray diffuse scattering during the 700 °C aging, heating to 1200 °C, and subsequent creep at 1250 °C, performed on both aged and quenched samples while simultaneously recording microhardness (ex-situ), dynamic modulus, and creep rate.
measurements: Intensity and correlation length of B2-type diffuse maxima around bcc reflections
Shear and Young’s moduli vs temperature
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If (a) no measurable SRO forms during 700 °C aging OR (b) aged samples show ≥10 % hardness/modulus increase without corresponding SRO signatures OR (c) SRO persists at 1250 °C yet creep rate is unchanged, the hypothesis is falsified.
